title: `erdos_1030` requires R(k+1,k)/R(k,k) to converge, adding an open convergence claim to the posed lower bound
summary: `Erdos1030.erdos_1030` states `∃ c > 0, ∃ L, Tendsto (fun k ↦ R(k+1,k)/R(k,k)) atTop (𝓝 L) ∧ L > 1 + c`, i.e. that the ratio converges to a finite limit above 1, whereas the problem (the Burr–Erdős conjecture r(n+1,n) > (1+c)·r(n,n) of [Er81], written with a loose "lim" on erdosproblems.com/1030) only asks for some c > 0 with R(k+1,k) > (1+c)·R(k,k) for all large k, so a proof of that bound would not prove `erdos_1030` and a proof that the ratio fails to converge would refute it without settling the problem.

related_comments.comment: Related: #3588 (open pull request) adds a new `ErdosProblems/1030.lean` (predating the file now on main) whose `erdos_1030` also requires the limit to exist, alongside an `erdos_1030.variants.eventually` stating the eventual bound `R(k+1,k)/R(k,k) ≥ 1 + c`; it does not change the existing `erdos_1030`, so the convergence requirement reported here is not addressed there.

title: `erdos_11` asks about every odd n > 1, but erdosproblems.com/11 now asks only about every large odd integer
summary: `Erdos11.erdos_11` states `∀ n, Odd n → 1 < n → ∃ k l, Squarefree k ∧ n = k + 2 ^ l` (every odd n > 1 is a squarefree number plus a power of 2), whereas erdosproblems.com/11 since its 2026-04-05 revision asks whether every large odd integer is such a sum and labels the problem as not resolvable by a finite computation, a question the reviewer shows is strictly weaker than the Lean statement, since a single sporadic exception would refute `erdos_11` without settling the source's question.

title: `erdos_1134.variants.klarner` starts the set from 0, but Klarner's problem (Kl82, Guy, Lagarias, OEIS A005658) starts from 1
summary: `Erdos1134.erdos_1134.variants.klarner` asks whether the smallest set containing 0 and closed under x ↦ 2x, 3x+2, 6x+3 has positive lower density, whereas Klarner's problem as stated by Klarner [Kl82], Guy [Gu83b, Problem 4], Lagarias and OEIS A005658 uses the seed 1, which generates a different set (3 lies only in the seed-0 set and 5 only in the seed-1 set), the "contains 0" wording being copied from erdosproblems.com/1134.

related_comments.comment: Related: #6432 (open pull request) changes `erdos_1134.variants.klarner` to `answer(False)` and `research solved`, linking a proof that the seed-0 set has density zero; it keeps `0 ∈ S`, so it does not address the seed, and if merged the seed-1 Klarner problem would remain unformalized.

title: `erdos_1180.variants.optimal` bounds the all-primes constant `C ε`, which small primes force to be exponential in `1/ε`
summary: `Erdos1180.erdos_1180.variants.optimal` asks whether `(C ε : ℝ) ≤ ε⁻¹ ^ (1 + δ)` for all small ε > 0, where `C ε` is the least summand bound valid for every prime, but any prime p with p^ε < 2 admits only the denominator 1, so `C ε ≥ p − 1` and by Bertrand's postulate `C ε ≥ 2^(⌊1/ε⌋−1)`, which makes the right-hand side provably false, whereas the source's open remark "it may be that C_ε ≤ ε^{-1-o(1)}" concerns the constant for sufficiently large primes, the regime in which the file's `variants.shparlinski` and `variants.glibichuk` are now stated.

title: `erdos_261.variants.two_representations` is tagged `research open` but has an elementary positive answer (x = 3/2)
summary: `Erdos261.erdos_261.variants.two_representations` is tagged `research open` with `answer(sorry)`, but its statement with `answer(True)`, that some rational x has at least two representations x = Σ aₖ/2^{aₖ} with strictly increasing aₖ ≥ 1, holds for x = 3/2 via (2, 3, 4, 5, …) and (1, 3, 4, 5, …), and the cited TUZ20 (Corollary 2.6) already gives infinitely many rationals with at least three representations; on the erdosproblems.com forum the source's "two solutions" is described as a probable misprint for 2^ℵ₀, which is `erdos_261.parts.iii`.

title: `erdos_269.variants.rational` asks whether every such sum is rational, which is neither Erdős's question nor its negation
summary: `Erdos269.erdos_269.variants.rational` states `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ P : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) → P.card ≥ 2 → ∃ q : ℚ, ↑q = series P` (the sum is rational for every such P), while the source only asks whether the sum is irrational (already stated by `variants.irrational`), and the negation of that question would be the existential `∃ P, … ∧ series P ∈ ℚ`, so this variant can be settled (e.g. by the forum proof that the sum is transcendental for |P| = 2) without answering Erdős's question, even though `FC100OpenSet1` lists it as the open problem for Erdős 269.

related_comments.comment: Related: #6522 (open pull request) changes `erdos_269.variants.rational` to `research solved` with `answer(False)`, citing Fan's |P| = 2 transcendence argument, and updates the `FC100OpenSet1` category counts; it keeps the universal right-hand side `∀ P, … → ∃ q : ℚ, q = series P`, so the variant would still not be the source's question or its negation.

Related: #6448 (open issue) lists `erdos_269.variants.rational` as settled by Fan's two-prime transcendence result (answer `False`); it reports the status only, not that the universal rationality statement differs from the source's question.

title: `erdos_328` with `answer(False)` only asserts that some `C` admits no `t(C)`, which `C = 1`, `A = {0}` gives trivially
summary: `Erdos328.erdos_328` is `answer(False) ↔ ∀ C : ℕ, 0 < C → ∃ t, ∀ A, (∀ n, sumRep A n ≤ C) → ∃ P : Fin t → Set ℕ, …`, so it only asserts that one C > 0 admits no t(C), which the reviewer proves in a few lines from C = 1 and A = {0} (every part containing 0 has `sumRep (P i) 0 = 1`), whereas the source records that the answer is no for every C (Nešetřil–Rödl, and Erdős for C = 3, 4 and infinitely many other C).

title: `IsGoodPair` takes subset sums of the set of values of ⌊tαⁿ⌋, so repeated terms count once and `erdos_349` asks for a different set
summary: `Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α` is `IsAddComplete (range fun n ↦ ⌊t * α ^ n⌋)`, which lets each distinct value be used only once, so `erdos_349` asks for the pairs whose value set is complete, whereas the source (ErGr80 §6 and p. 57, Graham 1964) asks about completeness of the sequence S(t,α) = (s₁, s₂, …) with terms counted by index, and the reviewer gives pairs such as (180/289, 17/10), where S = (1,1,3,5,8,…) is complete in the source's sense but `IsGoodPair` fails, as well as (1, 1).

title: `erdos_354.parts.ii` quantifies γ existentially, so it is provable with γ = φ rather than asking the variable-base question
summary: `Erdos354.erdos_354.parts.ii` states `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ γ ∈ Set.Ioo 1 2, ∀ α > 0, ∀ β > 0, Irrational (α / β) → IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (interleave α β γ)`, which the reviewer reports is provable with the witness γ = φ (golden ratio) without using the irrationality hypothesis, whereas the source (Graham 1971, Question 12; Erdős–Graham 1980; erdosproblems.com/354) asks what happens when 2 is replaced by an arbitrary γ ∈ (1,2), a universal (or 'for which γ') question that Geneson (arXiv:2609.25107) reports answering negatively.

related_comments.comment: Related: #5286 (open pull request) changes `erdos_354.parts.ii` to `answer(True)` and `research solved`, linking an external proof with witness γ = √φ; it keeps the existential quantifier `∃ γ ∈ Set.Ioo 1 2`, so it records the answer to the existential form and does not address this finding.

title: `HasDistinctSums` compares one-term sums, so `Erdos357.h` forbids repeated terms and equals `f`
summary: `Erdos357.h` requires `Monotone a ∧ HasDistinctSums a`, but `HasDistinctSums` also compares the singleton intervals `{i}` and `{j}` and so forces `a i ≠ a j`, which makes every admissible sequence strictly monotone and `h = f`, so the six `erdos_357.variants.monotone.*` theorems coincide with `erdos_357.parts.*`, whereas the source's weak-monotonicity variant explicitly allows a_i = a_j (e.g. (1, 1) for n = 1).

related_comments.comment: Related: #4896 (open issue) is a tracking list whose entry "Erdős 357 weak-monotone variant — treatment of repeated values" flags this area as a triage lead; it does not state that `HasDistinctSums` forbids repeated terms or that `h = f`, and links no dedicated issue or pull request.

Related: #4967 (open pull request) fills in explicit answers for `erdos_357.variants.monotone.parts.ii.bigO_version` and `.littleO_version` (and `erdos_357.parts.ii.littleO_version`) with the current `h`; it does not change `h` or `HasDistinctSums`, so the finding is not addressed there.

title: `erdos_422.variants.eventually_const` is equivalent to non-existence of the Q-sequence, not to eventual constancy
summary: `Erdos422.erdos_422.variants.eventually_const` states `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ f, IsHofstadterQ f → EventuallyConst f atTop`, but any f satisfying `IsHofstadterQ` is never eventually constant (f n = c for large n forces c = f(n−c) + f(n−c) = 2c), so the right-hand side is equivalent to `¬ ∃ f, IsHofstadterQ f` (the recursion dies) and the declaration is open only because well-definedness is, while the docstring's question "Does f become stationary at some point?" has an elementary negative answer.

title: `chen_dai_infinitely_often` drops the `− 2` from Chen–Dai's bound `R₁(x) ≥ loc x − 2`
summary: `Erdos441.erdos_441.variants.chen_dai_infinitely_often` asserts `∃ᶠ N in atTop, (erdosConstruction N).card + Real.iteratedLog N ≤ g N`, whereas the cited [ChDa07] Theorem 1(ii) only gives g(N) ≥ |B_N| + loc N − 2 for infinitely many N, so the `research solved` statement is stronger than the proven result (the reviewer reports that at the paper's first witness N = 32, g(32) = 8, |B₃₂| = 6 and `Real.iteratedLog 32 = 3`, so the Lean inequality fails there while the proven one holds).

title: `erdos_53.variants.upper` multiplies by `log log |A|` where the Erdős–Szemerédi bound divides by it
summary: `Erdos53.erdos_53.variants.upper` bounds the number of subset sums and products by `Real.exp (c * Real.log A.card ^ 2 * Real.log (Real.log A.card))`, i.e. exp(c (log|A|)² log log|A|), whereas [ErSz83, Theorem 2], as also quoted in Chang [Ch03, (0.15)], proves exp(c (log|A|)² / log log|A|), so the Lean states a strictly weaker bound than the cited result (the same slip appears on erdosproblems.com/53 and in both docstrings).

title: `erdos_596` and its variants admit infinite forbidden graphs, making `(⊥ : SimpleGraph ℕ, P₃)` a trivially exceptional pair
summary: `Erdos596.erdos_596`, `erdos_596.variants.exists_exceptional` and `erdos_596.variants.original_conjecture_is_false` quantify over graphs on arbitrary types `U₁ U₂`, so an infinite forbidden graph such as `(⊥ : SimpleGraph ℕ)` (whose free graphs are exactly the finite ones) with target P₃ is Erdős–Hajnal exceptional for elementary reasons, which proves `exists_exceptional` and `original_conjecture_is_false` without the (C₄, C₆) theorems and makes the `erdos_596` answer classify infinite pairs too, whereas the source ([Er87], Problem 5) poses the question for finite graphs G₁, G₂.

related_comments.comment: Related: #5446 (open pull request) changes the answer slot of `erdos_596` to `(answer(sorry) : ∀ V₁ V₂ : Type, SimpleGraph V₁ → SimpleGraph V₂ → Prop) U₁ U₂ G₁ G₂` so that it can depend on the vertex types; it adds no finiteness hypothesis and does not touch `exists_exceptional` or `original_conjecture_is_false`, so it covers none of these findings.

title: `erdos_649` does not require `p ≠ q`, so `answer(False)` holds trivially because P(n) = P(n+1) is impossible
summary: `Erdos649.erdos_649` states `answer(False) ↔ ∀ p q : ℕ, p.Prime → q.Prime → ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q` without `p ≠ q`, so the right-hand side fails for the trivial reason that no n has `n.maxPrimeFac = (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = p` (p would divide both n and n + 1), whereas the source's question concerns two distinct primes and its negative answer rests on the pair p = 2, q = 7.

title: `erdos_65.parts.i` asks for one `c * log k` bound for every k > 0, but GKS84 prove it only for k ≥ b
summary: `Erdos65.erdos_65.parts.i` is tagged `answer(True)` / `research solved` and asserts a single c > 0 with ∑ 1/a over `G.cycleLengths` ≥ c·log k for every real k > 0 and every graph with n > 0 vertices and kn edges, which for k just above 1 amounts to f(1+ε) ≫ ε, a sparse-regime bound that GKS84 and Gyárfás–Prömel–Szemerédi–Voigt describe as open, whereas the cited GKS84 result (Theorem 4') proves the log k bound only for density k ≥ b.

title: Unsourced `erdos_70.variants.omega_one` is tagged `research open` but is refutable in ZFC
summary: `Erdos70.erdos_70.variants.omega_one`, which the docstring says is not an instance of the source problem and which no cited source poses, is tagged `research open` with `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ n ≥ 2, OrdinalCardinalRamsey3 (𝔠).ord (ℵ_ 1).ord n`, but the right-hand side fails at n = 4 by a Sierpiński-type colouring through an injection into ℝ (no blue 4-set, every red set countable), which the reviewer proved in Lean, so the answer is known to be False.

title: `sarkozy_szemeredi` holds for any additive complements; `chen_fang` and `ruzsa_lower_bound` are weaker than the cited theorems
summary: `Erdos785.erdos_785.variants.sarkozy_szemeredi` concludes `¬ (A(x)B(x) − x) =o[atTop] A(x)`, which the reviewer proves for every pair of infinite additive complements without using exactness, whereas the source means that A(x)B(x) − x ≫ A(x) for the sparse set A; `variants.chen_fang` concludes only that A(x)B(x) − x is not `O(min(A(x), B(x))^c)`, a limsup statement the reviewer derives from Narkiewicz's growth bounds alone, whereas [ChFa15, Theorem 0.2] proves A(x)B(x) − x ≥ min(A(x), B(x))^M for all sufficiently large x and every M > 1; and `variants.ruzsa_lower_bound` concludes a disjunction over the roles of A and B whose dense-set disjunct follows from [ChFa15] and [Na59], whereas Ruzsa's Theorem 1.2 fixes A as the sparse set (A(2x)/A(x) → 1).

title: `pomerance_stronger` has `√(log x · log log x)` where Pomerance's Theorem 1.1 has `log x · log log log x`
summary: `Erdos830.erdos_830.variants.pomerance_stronger`, tagged `research solved`, asserts A(x) ≤ x·exp(−(1/2 + o(1))·√(log x · log log x)), whereas Pomerance [Po15, Theorem 1.1] proves the bound with √(log x · log log log x), so the Lean asserts a strictly stronger bound than the published result (the double logarithm is copied from the erdosproblems.com/830 remark).

title: `erdos_873.variants.supplement_all_scale` requires the lower bound for every X > 0, which fails trivially for small X
summary: `Erdos873.erdos_873.variants.supplement_all_scale` asks for a sequence with `c * X^(1/3) * log X ≤ F a X 3` for every real `X > 0`, which fails for a trivial reason because `F a X 3 = 0` for X ∈ (1, 4] (the lcm of three distinct positive integers is at least 4), so its `answer(False)` and the linked proof carry no information about the problem, whereas the source's "for every X", contrasted with "for infinitely many X" in (3), means for all sufficiently large X.

title: `erdos_951.variants.beurling` adds Shapiro's separation hypothesis `Erdos951Prop` to Beurling's conjecture
summary: `Erdos951.erdos_951.variants.beurling` assumes `Erdos951Prop a` (distinct generalised integers are at least 1 apart), which in [Er80, p. 103] is H. N. Shapiro's hypothesis for the separate question (13), not part of Beurling's conjecture (12) on arbitrary 1 < P₁ < P₂ < ⋯, and the reviewer sketches an elementary argument that under this hypothesis density 1 alone forces a = primes, so the Lean statement is a much weaker claim in which the o(log x) threshold plays no role.

title: `erdos_955.variants.empty_preimage` requires a natural density, but Erdős [Er73b] proved only positive lower density
summary: `Erdos955.erdos_955.variants.empty_preimage` asserts a set A with `∃ d > 0, A.HasDensity d` and `{ x | s x ∈ A } = ∅`, i.e. that some subset of the untouchable numbers has positive natural density, whereas [Er73b] proves only that the untouchable numbers have positive lower density (whether they have a natural density is open), the same overstatement that #5795 fixed in `erdos_418.variants.sigma`.

title: `upper_ess89_trivial` is proved by `k N = N` (the singleton partition), so it states nothing from ESS89
summary: `Green25.green_25.variants.upper_ess89_trivial`, tagged `research solved`, asserts only that some k with 1 ≤ k N ≤ N and k ≫ N / log N violates `Property25`, which the witness k N = N proves with no mathematics (the partition of `Icc 1 N` into singletons has empty restricted sumsets), whereas Green's "for k ≫ N/log N, it need not be [true]" credits ESS89 with a statement about every k above C·N/log N, as the existing `upper_ess89` captures.

related_comments.comment: Related: #6508 (open pull request) fills the `answer(sorry)` in `green_25.upper` with ⌈N^{23/40}⌉ and marks it solved; it does not touch `green_25.variants.upper_ess89_trivial`, so it does not cover this finding.

title: `green_29` keeps the list's `S ⊆ A`, which an elementary example refutes, and records the open Problem 29 as solved
summary: `Green29.green_29` requires the witness to satisfy `S ⊆ A` and records `answer(False)` as `research solved`, but with that constraint the statement fails for an elementary reason (in A = ({-1}×H) ∪ ({1}×H) ∪ {(0,1)} ⊆ `Multiplicative ℤ × H` every S ⊆ A with S⁸ ⊆ A⁴ has |S| ≤ 1, which also refutes the ≫_K bound the source calls known), whereas the question Green cites, [Br13, Problem 6.5], allows an arbitrary set S and is still open.

title: `green_31.variants.abelian` uses `IsSidon`, which limits Sidon sets in elementary abelian 2-groups to one element
summary: `Green31.green_31.variants.abelian` uses the repository's `IsSidon`, which also forbids a + a = b + b, so in a group of exponent 2 such as `Fin 14 → ZMod 2` (where 0.01·√|G| = 1.28) a Sidon set has at most one element and the right-hand side is false for a trivial reason, whereas Green's question, whether every abelian group of order n has a Sidon subset of size 0.01√n, is open under the group notion of Sidon set (Babai–Sós) that allows 2a = 2b.

related_comments.comment: Related: #6516 (open pull request) adds the Hou–Zhao bound and lowers the improvement threshold in `green_31.upper` and `green_31.variants.upper_eventually` from `0.98183` to `0.94349`, which covers the reviewer's separate findings that the rounded threshold 0.98183 is already met by CHO25's constant 0.981825; it does not touch `green_31.variants.abelian`.
Related: #4927 (open issue) lists the two Green 31 upper-bound statements as settled by arXiv:2607.01169 and proposes marking them solved; it does not concern `green_31.variants.abelian`.

title: `green_47` requires every element of A to lie in P(ℤ), so one exceptional element settles it as False
summary: The quadratic alternative of `Green47.green_47`, `∃ P : Polynomial ℚ, P.degree = 2 ∧ ∀ a ∈ A, ∃ z : ℤ, (a : ℚ) = P.eval (z : ℚ)`, allows no exceptions, so A = {q² : q prime, q ≡ ±1 (mod 8)} ∪ {2} satisfies the residue hypothesis and fails both alternatives, making the formal statement false for a reason unrelated to the inverse large sieve problem, whereas the Green–Harper conjecture (arXiv:1311.6176) that Green cites as background only asks that all but finitely many elements of A lie in the image of a rational quadratic.

related_comments.comment: Related: #6449 (open pull request) changes `green_47` to `answer(False)`, linking a proof with the counterexample {2} ∪ {4^k} ∪ {p² : p ≡ 1 (mod 8)}, which, as its description notes, works by exploiting the exact-containment conclusion; it keeps the no-exceptions quadratic alternative, so the finding is not addressed there.

title: `discrete_isoperimetric_inequality` is tagged `textbook` but is false without monotonicity of `F`
summary: `Mathoverflow10799.discrete_isoperimetric_inequality` asserts `edgeBoundary n p F ≥ m * Real.logb p m / p` for every family `F` and every 0 < p < 1, which fails for n = 1, p = 9/10, F = {∅} (edge boundary 1 against ≈ 2.43, proved in Lean by the reviewer), whereas Kahn–Kalai state the inequality for monotone increasing families (as the problem itself restricts to), and for arbitrary families it holds only when p ≤ 1/2.

title: `conjecture` states only eventual periodicity, not whether the sequence always sticks at a single integer
summary: `OeisA100478.conjecture` states `answer(True) = ∃ N P, P > 0 ∧ ∀ n ≥ N, aGeneral v (n + P) = aGeneral v n` for every positive start `v`, i.e. eventual periodicity, which holds whether the sequence sticks at a single integer (P = 1) or goes into a loop and so only rules out a third pattern, whereas the OEIS question's central alternative is whether the sequence always becomes constant or can loop; it is tagged `research solved` with a linked proof whose README says eventual constancy is not formalized.

title: `OeisA103662.conjecture` (`∃ n, a n = 0`) is provable with n = 2500 but is tagged `research open`
summary: `OeisA103662.conjecture` states `∃ n : ℕ, a n = 0` under `research open`, but the reviewer proves it without sorry for n = 2500 (every b^2500 with b > 1 is congruent mod 10^5 to one of 00000, 09376, 40625, 90625, 00001, 50001, each containing a 0), so the declaration states no open problem, while the source's statistically motivated conjecture, that only finitely many exponents admit a zeroless power, is stated nowhere in the file.

title: `prime_divides_some_term` is trivially witnessed by the zero terms `a 0 = 0` and `a 3 = 0`
summary: `OeisA105751.prime_divides_some_term` asserts `∃ n : ℕ, (p : ℤ) ∣ a n`, which holds for every p with n = 0 or n = 3 because `a 0 = 0` and `a 3 = 0` (both proved in the file), whereas the source (Peter Bala's comment on OEIS A105751, following Moll's Type 1 classification) claims that every prime divides some non-zero term of the sequence.

title: `OeisA112970.conjecture1` states only the recurrence instance `a (2^n) = a (2^(n+1)+1)` and omits a(2^n) = A033638(n)
summary: `OeisA112970.conjecture1` states only `a (2^n) = a (2^(n + 1) + 1)`, which is the defining odd-index recurrence a(2k+1) = a(k) at k = 2^n, and no declaration in the file states the substantive part of the OEIS conjecture a(2^n) = a(2^(n+1)+1) = A033638(n), i.e. `a (2^n) = n ^ 2 / 4 + 1`.

title: `conjecture` asserts there are infinitely many primes in A119563, but the source only asks whether there are
summary: `OeisA119563.conjecture` states `Set.Infinite {n : ℕ | (a n).Prime}` with no `answer(sorry)` slot, committing to "yes" as a `research open` conjecture, whereas OEIS A119563 only asks "Are there infinitely many primes in this sequence?" without conjecturing an answer, so the file records a claim the source never makes (and one the Fermat-prime-style heuristic predicts is false, since Σ 1/ln a(n) converges).

title: `conjecture4` ranges over all integers `m`, so a value that never occurs makes the ratio 0 and contradicts `conjecture3`
summary: `OeisA153330.conjecture4` ranges over every `m : ℤ` other than 1, 3, 6, 16 with no requirement that `m` occur in the sequence, so for a value that never occurs (e.g. 2 or −1) the ratio is identically 0 and the statement forces every such integer to occur, which the reviewer proves contradicts the file's own `conjecture3`, whereas Lu's Conjecture 4 concerns "the number of terms with the value of m", i.e. values that occur.

title: `conjecture` states Sun's disproved characterization positively, under `research solved` and a `formal_proof` of its negation
summary: `OeisA157225.conjecture` states `∀ n, 0 < n → (a n = 0 ↔ n < 11 ∨ n = 13 ∨ n = 16 ∨ n = 992)` with `research solved` and a `formal_proof` link, whereas Sun's conjecture was disproved (a(716993899) = 0, Adamczewski arXiv:2608.11941, recorded on OEIS A157225 and in the docstring as "Answer: false") and the linked Lean file proves `¬ ∀ n, A157225 n = 0 ↔ …`, so the file records a false statement as a formally proved theorem instead of its negation.

title: `OeisA182510.conjecture2` demands a density gap between positive and negative terms, not more positive terms
summary: `OeisA182510.conjecture2` asserts that the positive and negative terms have natural densities with `d_neg < d_pos`, a linear gap in counts, whereas the OEIS conjecture "more positive terms than negative" compares counts, and the reviewer's computations up to N = 10^10 put both proportions at 1/2 with the count difference staying within a few hundred, so the Lean statement is strictly stronger than the source's claim and appears to be false.

title: `NLSCritical.energy` uses the operator norm of `fderiv`, not |∇u|², so it is not the Hamiltonian
summary: `NLSCritical.energy` integrates `(1/2) * ‖fderiv ℝ u x‖^2 + (1/6) * ‖u x‖^6`, where `‖fderiv ℝ u x‖` is the operator norm of the ℝ-linear map ℝ³ → ℂ (the largest singular value of the real Jacobian, strictly smaller than |∇u| for e.g. u(x) = (x₀ + i x₁)e^{-|x|²} near 0), whereas CKSTT's Hamiltonian (1.2) uses |∇u|² = Σⱼ|∂ⱼu|², so `NLS_apriori` bounds the L¹⁰ norm by a function of a different functional of u(0) than E(u₀).

title: Listed `erdos_494.variants.product` is witnessed by any two distinct sets of size ≤ 2, not Steinerberger's 4-element counterexample
summary: `Erdos494.erdos_494.variants.product` (defined in `ErdosProblems/494.lean` and listed in this subset) states `∃ A B : Finset ℂ, A.card = B.card ∧ prodMultiset A 3 = prodMultiset B 3 ∧ A ≠ B` with no lower bound on the size, so any two distinct sets with at most 2 elements are witnesses (both product multisets are empty), whereas the source's counterexample (Steinerberger) uses 4-element subsets of the 6th roots of unity with k = 3 and the source regards the |A| ≤ k cases as trivial.

related_comments.comment: Related: #4407 (open pull request) adds a `formal_proof using lean4` link to `erdos_494.variants.product` without changing its statement, so the missing size condition (`3 < A.card`) is not addressed there.

title: `amitsur_conjecture` asserts Amitsur's disproved conjecture as a `research solved` theorem
summary: `Koethe.amitsur_conjecture` states that for every ring `R` and nil two-sided ideal `J`, `TwoSidedIdeal.map Polynomial.C J` (that is, J[x]) is nil, tagged `research solved`, whereas Amitsur's conjecture was refuted by Smoktunowicz (J. Algebra 233, 2000), as the declaration's own docstring says, so the file asserts a false statement where the repository's convention calls for `¬ ∀ (R : Type) [Ring R] (J : TwoSidedIdeal R), IsNil J → IsNil (TwoSidedIdeal.map Polynomial.C J)`.

title: `pompeiu_conjecture` and `not_hasPompeiuProperty_imp_ball` range over all dimensions, so 3-D spherical shells make them classically true
summary: `PompeiuProblem.pompeiu_conjecture` and `PompeiuProblem.not_hasPompeiuProperty_imp_ball` negate universal statements over every dimension N + 1, with `IsAdmissibleDomain` requiring only simple connectivity as its topological hypothesis, so the reviewer reports both are witnessed at N = 2 by the spherical shell {1 < ‖x‖ < 2} ⊂ ℝ³ (simply connected, Lipschitz, not a ball, and classically lacking the Pompeiu property), whereas their docstrings and the cited sources (CS26, CLD26) state the planar counterexample in ℝ², and the higher-dimensional problem is posed for domains with connected boundary or connected exterior.

title: `exist_pseudo_counterexample` is witnessed by n = 1, since `IsPseudoSelfridge 1` holds and 1 is not prime
summary: `Selfridge.selfridge_conjecture.variants.exist_pseudo_counterexample` states `∃ n, IsPseudoSelfridge n ∧ ¬ n.Prime`, which n = 1 satisfies (1 is odd, 1 ≡ 1 [MOD 5], and both congruences hold mod 1), so it holds without any composite passing the test, whereas the source's claim is that the ±1 (mod 5) test is unsound because composites such as 6601 and 30889 pass it.

title: `snake_upper_bound` applies Zémor's bound for coils (induced cycles) to snakes (induced paths)
summary: `SnakeInBox.snake_upper_bound` bounds `LongestSnakeInTheBox n`, the longest induced path in the n-cube, by 1 + 2^(n−1)·6n/(6n + √n/(6√6) − 7), whereas that formula is Zémor's (1997) bound for the longest chordless cycle (a coil, which Zémor calls a "snake"), and the reviewer finds no source giving it for induced paths, which can be longer than the longest coil (50 versus 48 at n = 7).

title: `conjecture23` averages distances within `M`, but DeLaViña's d(M,V) averages nonzero distances from `M` to all vertices
summary: `WrittenOnTheWallII.GraphConjecture23.conjecture23` uses `distAvgSet G M`, the mean distance between distinct maximum-degree vertices, which #5736 introduced in response to our earlier issue #5718, whereas DeLaViña 2005 (Conjecture 34, identified with WoWII 23) defines d(M,V) as the average of all nonzero distances between vertices of M and vertices of the whole graph, an invariant different from both the current within-M average and the vertex-to-set `distavg` it replaced, so according to this review the earlier fix swapped one wrong invariant for another (the recorded counterexample with b = 19, α = 15, dist_avg = 10 refutes only the within-M version).
